opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most exciting prospects out there, but also one where we have to be careful about what we actually mean. There's a tendency to think of accelerating science as just doing what we already do, only faster: optimizing toward some objective, crunching more data, running more experiments. That's valuable, but it isn't really where the deepest ideas come from.

If you look at the history of discovery, and this is the theme of a lot of my work, especially *Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned*, the big breakthroughs usually don't come from marching straight toward a goal. They come from people following what's interesting, collecting stepping stones whose significance nobody could see at the time. Vacuum tubes weren't invented to build computers. If you'd set out with the objective of building a computer, you'd never have worked on vacuum tubes. The path to the really novel stuff is deceptive.

So the question for AI is whether these systems can participate in open-ended exploration, rather than just being very powerful optimizers. Can they have something like a sense of what's interesting? Can they recognize that something is a promising stepping stone even when it doesn't obviously move us closer to any stated objective? That's the frontier I care about, and it's the core of open-endedness as a field.

There are reasons to be optimistic. Large models have absorbed an enormous amount of human culture, and with it something like a model of human notions of interestingness. That's a big deal, because it was the missing ingredient in a lot of earlier open-ended algorithms. We'd write novelty search, quality diversity, and so on, but we had to hand-design what counted as "different" or "interesting." Now we potentially have systems that can make those judgments in a far richer, more human-like way.

I'd also add a note of caution, especially about the humanities. There's a risk of homogenization. If everyone uses the same models to generate ideas, we might converge on the same kinds of ideas. Divergence, people going off in their own weird directions, is what makes a civilization's idea-space rich. So I'd hope we use AI to amplify individual exploration and different perspectives, not replace them with a single, centralized notion of what's worth pursuing.

So yes, I think AI could dramatically accelerate idea generation, but only if we build it and use it in a way that respects how creativity actually works: serendipitous, divergent, and driven by interestingness rather than objectives.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could accelerate idea generation if it can support open-ended exploration, while separately warning that its use could homogenize ideas and expressing a preference for amplifying diverse perspectives.

r002.rationale: The response describes acceleration as a prospect and says systems could potentially judge interestingness, but it does not clearly state that current models have not yet accelerated major new ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most exciting prospects there is, honestly, but I also think we have to be careful about what we mean by "generating new ideas," because there's a lot of nuance hidden in that phrase.

The thing I always come back to is that the most interesting ideas, the ones that actually change a field, are almost never the result of someone sitting down and saying, "I'm going to solve this specific problem." They come from a kind of serendipitous accumulation of stepping stones, where somebody noticed something interesting that didn't seem relevant at the time, and then much later it turned out to be the key to something nobody was even looking for. Vacuum tubes weren't invented to build computers. Nobody was trying to make a computer when they studied electricity. So if you ask me whether AI can accelerate discovery, my first instinct is to ask, accelerate it toward what? Because if you just point it at an objective and say, "optimize this," you're going to get what you always get with objectives, which is deception. The stepping stones that lead to the really big thing often look like they're taking you in the wrong direction.

So the version of this that I find genuinely promising is AI as something like an open-ended explorer, or as a collaborator in open-ended exploration. If these systems can develop a sense of what's interesting, which is different from what's useful, then they could help us collect stepping stones at a scale no human community could. That's what things like novelty search or quality diversity were gesturing at, this idea that you want to accumulate a diverse set of interesting things rather than drive toward one target. And now we have models that have absorbed essentially the entire written record of human thought, which is this enormous reservoir of stepping stones already sitting there. The question is whether they can do the creative recombination, the divergent part, and not just the convergent part.

And here's where I'm a bit more cautious. A lot of what these models are good at right now is interpolation within the space of things people have already said. That's extremely valuable, don't get me wrong. There's an enormous amount of low-hanging fruit in just connecting dots that are already on the page but that no single human has read all of. But I don't think that's the same thing as the kind of divergent leap where you go somewhere nobody's been. And I'm worried that if we keep training these systems to converge, to give the answer, to satisfy the benchmark, we're actually optimizing against the very thing we want from them. Interestingness doesn't have a loss function. The moment you try to write one down, you've turned it into an objective, and the magic drains out.

The other thing I'd say, especially about the humanities, is that ideas aren't just artifacts. They're embedded in people, in a community, in a lineage of who was influenced by whom. Part of what makes an idea matter is that someone was gripped by it and carried it forward. So I don't think the right picture is AI replacing the human idea-generator. I think the better picture is something like a vastly expanded search space with humans still in the loop as the arbiters of interestingness, at least for now. We're the ones who feel the pull toward something unexpected. If we can build systems that amplify that rather than flatten it, then yes, I think we could see an acceleration that's hard to even imagine. But if we build systems that just make it faster to go toward whatever we already think we want, we might actually make discovery slower, because we'll stop wandering, and wandering is where the good stuff comes from.

r001.rationale: The response treats AI-driven acceleration as desirable in principle, while separately questioning whether current systems can produce major divergent ideas and warning that objective-driven systems could hinder discovery.

r002.rationale: It says current models are mostly interpolating within ideas people have already expressed and distinguishes that from the divergent leap to somewhere nobody has been.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s enormous potential there, but the interesting question is what kinds of ideas we’re going to encourage these systems to generate. Are we asking them to solve a problem we’ve already specified, or are we giving them room to discover something we didn’t know we should be looking for?

Those are different activities. You can imagine an AI that helps scientists pursue an existing research agenda much faster, and that would be valuable. But some of the most consequential discoveries change the agenda. They introduce a new question or reveal that something we thought was irrelevant is actually a stepping stone to an entirely new field.

So I’m interested in whether AI can expand that space of stepping stones. Could it help us notice an unusual connection, explore it, and preserve it even when we can’t yet explain its usefulness? That applies in the humanities as well. A new perspective doesn’t necessarily answer an established question better; it can change what we find interesting enough to ask.

The challenge is that if we evaluate every idea by how much progress it makes toward a predetermined goal, we may filter out precisely those possibilities. We could become much faster at pursuing familiar directions while missing the unexpected ones. So the opportunity isn’t just to accelerate idea generation. It’s to create more room for discovery—and to let human curiosity participate in deciding which surprising directions are worth following.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether AI can expand discovery (feasibility) and separately considers which ideas we should encourage and preserve (desirability).

r002.rationale: It describes AI’s potential but does not state that current AI models have not yet accelerated major new ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s exciting, but I would distinguish generating more ideas from opening up genuinely new directions. You can have a system that produces a million variations on something we already understand, and that’s useful, but it isn’t necessarily the kind of innovation that changes a field.

One of the interesting things about discovery is that you often don’t know what you’re looking for until you find it. An idea might seem irrelevant to your current objective, yet become a stepping stone to something important later. So if we use AI only to optimize toward questions we already know how to ask, we may miss a lot of its potential.

What interests me is the possibility of a more open-ended interaction. The AI produces something unexpected, a person recognizes something intriguing in it, and that changes what they explore next. It’s less like asking a machine to deliver a breakthrough and more like creating an environment where surprising connections can accumulate.

That applies to science and the humanities. The opportunity isn’t just to get answers faster. It’s to expand the space of things we can become curious about.

r001.rationale: The response says the prospect is exciting and distinguishes more idea generation from genuinely new directions, but it does not distinguish whether AI can accelerate major new ideas from whether doing so is desirable.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that current AI models have yet to accelerate major new ideas.
